nodes.label: eq:l2normproj

nodes.name: (i) Orthogonality
nodes.statement: For (i) let $b^*(x) = \Omega^{-1/2} b(x)$ so that $\int b^* w(b^*)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } d\mathbb{P} = I$ and note that \begin{align*} \int ( \Pi_w f ) (I-\Pi_w) &g \ w d\mathbb{P} = \int \int b(x)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \Omega^{-1} b(t) f(t)g(x) \ wd\mathbb{P}(t) \ wd\mathbb{P}(x) \\ & \hspace{.9in} - \int b(x)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \Omega^{-1} b(t) f(t) b(x)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \Omega^{-1} b(u) g(u) \ wd\mathbb{P}(t) \ wd\mathbb{P}(x) \ wd\mathbb{P}(u) \\ &= \int b^*(x)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } b^*(t) f(t) g(x) \ wd\mathbb{P}(t) \ wd\mathbb{P}(x) \\ & \hspace{.9in} - \int f(t) b^*(t)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } b^*(x) b^*(x)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } b^*(u) g(u) \ wd\mathbb{P}(t) \ wd\mathbb{P}(x) \ wd\mathbb{P}(u) \\ &= \int b^*(x)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } b^*(t) f(t) g(x) \ wd\mathbb{P}(t) \ wd\mathbb{P}(x) \\ & \hspace{.9in} - \int f(t) b^*(t)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } b^*(u) g(u) \ wd\mathbb{P}(t) \ wd\mathbb{P}(u) = 0 \end{align*} where the last line follows since $\int b^*(x) b^*(x)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \ wd\mathbb{P}(x) = I$.
nodes.statement_short: Orthonormalize and expand.

nodes.name: (ii) Norm contraction
nodes.statement: For (ii) we have by definition that $\int \{\Pi_w f(x)\}^2 w(x) \ dF(x) $ equals \begin{align} \int &\left\{ \int f(u) w(u) b(u)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \ d\mathbb{P}(u) \Omega^{-1} b(x) \right\} \left\{ b(x)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \Omega^{-1} \int b(t) w(t) f(t) \ d\mathbb{P}(t) \right\} w(x) d\mathbb{P}(x) \nonumber \\ &= \left\{ \int f(u) w(u) b(u)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \ d\mathbb{P}(u) \Omega^{-1} \right\} \left\{ \int b(t) w(t) f(t) \ d\mathbb{P}(t) \right\} \\ &= \int f(t) \Pi_w f(t) w(t) \ d\mathbb{P}(t) \nonumber \end{align} and so \begin{align*} \int (f-\Pi_w f )^2 w \ d\mathbb{P} &= \int f^2 w \ d\mathbb{P} - 2 \int f \Pi_w f w \ d\mathbb{P} + \int (\Pi_w f)^2 w \ d\mathbb{P} \\ &= \int f^2 w \ d\mathbb{P} - \int (\Pi_w f)^2 w \ d\mathbb{P} \end{align*} which implies the results, as long as $w \geq 0$, so that the far left and right sides are non-negative.
nodes.statement_short: Pythagorean identity.

nodes.name: (iii) Coefficient norm
nodes.statement: For (iii) we have \begin{align*} \| \Omega^{1/2} \theta_{w,f} \|^2 &= ( \Omega^{1/2} \theta_{w,f} )^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } (\Omega^{1/2} \theta_{w,f}) = \theta_{w,f}^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \Omega \theta_{w,f} \\ &= \left( \int b^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } w f \ d\mathbb{P} \right) \Omega^{-1} \left( \int b w f \ d\mathbb{P} \right) \\ &= \int \{\Pi_w f(x)\}^2 w(x) \ d\mathbb{P}(x) \end{align*} where the last equality holds by \eqref{eq:l2normproj}, and so the result follows from Lemma \ref{lem:projections}(ii).
nodes.statement_short: Coefficient norm equals projection norm.

nodes.name: Eigenvalues and inverse error of Omega-hat
nodes.statement: Assume: \begin{enumerate} \item $0 < b \leq \lambda_{\min}(\Omega) \leq \lambda_{\max}(\Omega) \leq B < \infty$ \item $0 < c \leq \| d \widehat{F}^*/dF^* \|_\infty \leq C < \infty$ \end{enumerate} Then $$ bc \leq \lambda_{\min}(\widehat\Omega) \leq \lambda_{\max}(\widehat\Omega) \leq BC $$ and $$ \| \widehat\Omega^{-1} - \Omega^{-1} \| \leq \left( \frac{ B }{b^2 c} \right) \| (d\widehat{F}^*/dF^*) - 1 \|_\infty . $$
conclusions: $$ bc \leq \lambda_{\min}(\widehat\Omega) \leq \lambda_{\max}(\widehat\Omega) \leq BC $$
$$ \| \widehat\Omega^{-1} - \Omega^{-1} \| \leq \left( \frac{ B }{b^2 c} \right) \| (d\widehat{F}^*/dF^*) - 1 \|_\infty . $$
nodes.statement_short: Bounded density ratio of F-hat to F transfers eigenvalue bounds to Omega-hat and bounds the inverse error.
nodes.label: lem:eigen

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7
nodes.statement: The logic mirrors that of the proof of Proposition 2.1 in \citet{belloni2015some}. Note that \begin{align*} a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \widehat\Omega a &= \int \Big\{ a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } b(v) \Big\}^2 \ d\widehat{F}^*(v) \\ & \leq \| d\widehat{F}^*/dF^* \|_\infty \int \Big\{ a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } b(v) \Big\}^2 \ d{F}^*(v) \\ &= \| d\widehat{F}^*/dF^* \|_\infty \ a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \Omega a \end{align*} and by the same logic, $a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \Omega a \leq \| dF^*/d\widehat{F}^* \|_\infty \ a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \widehat\Omega a$. Therefore \begin{align*} \lambda_{\max}( \widehat\Omega) &= \max_{\|a \|=1} a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \widehat\Omega a \leq \| d\widehat{F}^*/dF^* \|_\infty \lambda_{\max}(\Omega) \\ \lambda_{\min}( \widehat\Omega) &= \min_{\|a \|=1} a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \widehat\Omega a \geq \| dF^*/d\widehat{F}^* \|_\infty^{-1} \lambda_{\min}(\Omega) \end{align*} by the min-max theorem, which gives the first inequality. For the second, note \begin{align*} \| \widehat\Omega^{-1} - \Omega^{-1} \| &= \| \widehat\Omega^{-1} (\Omega -\widehat\Omega ) \Omega^{-1} \| \\ &\leq \| \widehat\Omega^{-1} \| \| \Omega -\widehat\Omega \| \| \Omega^{-1} \| \end{align*} by the sub-multiplicative property of the operator norm, and then $$ \| \Omega -\widehat\Omega \| \leq \| (d\widehat{F}^*/dF^*) - 1 \|_\infty \ \| \Omega \| $$ by the same logic as above.
nodes.statement_short: Compare quadratic forms via the density ratio and apply the min-max theorem; then submultiplicativity.

nodes.name: Analogy with Belloni et al.
nodes.statement: The logic mirrors that of the proof of Proposition 2.1 in \citet{belloni2015some}.
nodes.statement_short: Follow Belloni et al.

nodes.name: Eigenvalue bounds
nodes.statement: Note that \begin{align*} a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \widehat\Omega a &= \int \Big\{ a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } b(v) \Big\}^2 \ d\widehat{F}^*(v) \\ & \leq \| d\widehat{F}^*/dF^* \|_\infty \int \Big\{ a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } b(v) \Big\}^2 \ d{F}^*(v) \\ &= \| d\widehat{F}^*/dF^* \|_\infty \ a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \Omega a \end{align*} and by the same logic, $a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \Omega a \leq \| dF^*/d\widehat{F}^* \|_\infty \ a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \widehat\Omega a$. Therefore \begin{align*} \lambda_{\max}( \widehat\Omega) &= \max_{\|a \|=1} a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \widehat\Omega a \leq \| d\widehat{F}^*/dF^* \|_\infty \lambda_{\max}(\Omega) \\ \lambda_{\min}( \widehat\Omega) &= \min_{\|a \|=1} a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \widehat\Omega a \geq \| dF^*/d\widehat{F}^* \|_\infty^{-1} \lambda_{\min}(\Omega) \end{align*} by the min-max theorem, which gives the first inequality.
nodes.statement_short: Quadratic forms and min-max theorem.

nodes.name: Inverse error bound
nodes.statement: For the second, note \begin{align*} \| \widehat\Omega^{-1} - \Omega^{-1} \| &= \| \widehat\Omega^{-1} (\Omega -\widehat\Omega ) \Omega^{-1} \| \\ &\leq \| \widehat\Omega^{-1} \| \| \Omega -\widehat\Omega \| \| \Omega^{-1} \| \end{align*} by the sub-multiplicative property of the operator norm, and then $$ \| \Omega -\widehat\Omega \| \leq \| (d\widehat{F}^*/dF^*) - 1 \|_\infty \ \| \Omega \| $$ by the same logic as above.
nodes.statement_short: Submultiplicativity bounds the inverse error.

nodes.name: Matching bounds for a covariate-density submodel
nodes.statement: More specifically, the lower and upper bounds match for a model in which the covariate density $dF(x)$ is known, satisfies $\int \mathbbold{1}\{ \|x-x_0 \| \leq h/2 \} \ dF(x) \asymp h^d$, and has local support $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^d: dF(x)>0, \|x-x_0\| \leq h/2 \}$ on a union of no more than $k$ disjoint cubes all with proportional volume, for $h$ and $k$ defined in Proposition \ref{prop:hellbound2}.
assumptions: the covariate density $dF(x)$ is known, satisfies $\int \mathbbold{1}\{ \|x-x_0 \| \leq h/2 \} \ dF(x) \asymp h^d$
conclusions: the lower and upper bounds match

nodes.name: Proof of matching bounds in the submodel
nodes.statement: The lower bounds come from Theorems \ref{thm:lowerbound} and \ref{thm:lowerbound2} since the density used in our construction satisfies these conditions, while the matching upper bound is implied by the results in Section \ref{sec:upperbound} together with the following lemma, in which we prove that Condition \ref{cnd:reg1} holds for this class of densities.
nodes.statement_short: Lower bounds from Theorems 1 and 3; upper bound from Section 4 plus Lemma 8.

nodes.name: Bounded eigenvalues for the covariate-density class
nodes.statement: Assume: \begin{enumerate} \item $dF(x)$ satisfies $\int \mathbbold{1}\{ \|x-x_0 \| \leq h/2 \} \ dF(x) \asymp h^d$, \item $dF(x)$ is bounded above and below away from zero on its local support $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^d: dF(x)>0, \|x-x_0\| \leq h/2 \}$, which is a union of no more than $k$ disjoint cubes all with proportional volume, for $h$ and $k$ defined in Proposition \ref{prop:hellbound2}. \end{enumerate} Let $dF^*(v)=dF(x_0 + h(v-1/2))$ denote the distribution in $\mathcal{B}_h(x_0)$, the $h$-ball around $x_0$, mapped to $[0,1]^d$, and similarly for $\pi^*$. Then the eigenvalues of $$ Q = \int \rho(v) \rho(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \pi^*(v) \{ 1-\pi^*(v)\}\ dF^*(v) $$ are bounded above and below away from zero, and there exists a basis $b$ with \text{H\"{o}lder}{} approximation property \eqref{eq:holder}, for which the eigenvalues of $$ \Omega = \int b(v) b(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \ dF^*(v) $$ are bounded above and below away from zero.
conclusions: are bounded above and below away from zero, and there exists a basis $b$ with \text{H\"{o}lder}{} approximation property \eqref{eq:holder},
nodes.statement_short: For densities supported on at most k proportional cubes near x_0, Q and Omega (for a constructed basis) have bounded eigenvalues.
nodes.label: lem:covdensity

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8
nodes.statement: Note that since $\epsilon(1-\epsilon) \leq \pi(1-\pi) \leq 1/4$ and since $dF(x)$ is bounded above and below on its support, the eigenvalues of $Q$ will be bounded if those of the matrix $$ \sum_{j=1}^k \int \rho(v) \rho(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv $$ are, where $M_j$ indicates the $j$th disjoint cube making up the local support of $F$. By the min-max theorem, the eigenvalues are bounded by the min and max of $$ a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \int \rho(v) \rho(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \sum_j \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv \ a = \int \Big\{ a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \rho(v) \Big\}^2 \sum_j \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv $$ over all $a \in \mathbb{R}^q$ with $\| a\|=1$. First consider lower bounding the eigenvalues. Note $g(v) = a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \rho(v)$ is a polynomial of degree at most $q$. Therefore \begin{align*} \sum_j \int g(v)^2 \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv &\geq \int g(v)^2 \mathbbold{1}\{ g(v)^2 \geq \epsilon \} \sum_j \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv \\ & \geq \epsilon \int \mathbbold{1}\{ g(v)^2 \geq \epsilon \} \sum_j \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv \\ & \geq \epsilon \left\{ \sum_j \int \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv - \int \mathbbold{1}\{ g(v)^2 < \epsilon \} \ dv \right\} \\ & \geq \epsilon \left( C^* - C \epsilon^{1/2q} \right) = \left( \frac{C^*}{\sqrt{C}} \right)^{4q} > 0 \end{align*} where the last line follows since \begin{align*} \int \sum_j \mathbbold{1}( v \in M_j) \ dv & \asymp \int dF^*(v) = \int dF(x_0 + h(v-1/2)) \\ &= h^{-d} \int \mathbbold{1}\{ \|x-x_0 \| \leq h/2 \} \ dF(x) \geq C^* \end{align*} from a change of variables $x = x_0 + h(v-1/2)$, so that $v = 1/2 + (x-x_0)/h$ and $h^d \ dv = dx$, together with Assumption 1 of the lemma, and by Theorem 4 of \citet{carbery2001distributional}. The last equality follows if we choose $\epsilon =\left( C^*/2C \right)^{2q}$. To upper-bound the eigenvalues, note that \begin{align*} \int \Big\{ a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \rho(v) \Big\}^2 \sum_j \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv \leq \int \Big\{ a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \rho(v) \Big\}^2 \ dv = \| a \|^2 = 1 \end{align*} since $\int \rho(v) \rho(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \ dv = I$ by the orthonormality of $\rho$. \\ Now consider the eigenvalues of $\Omega$. We will construct a basis of order $k$ for which eigenvalues of $\Omega$ are bounded and for which the \text{H\"{o}lder}{} approximation property \eqref{eq:holder} holds. \\ \begin{remark} For simplicity we only consider the case where there are exactly $k$ cubes in the local support of $F$; if there are finitely many cubes, say $M < \infty$, the arguments are more straightforward, orthonormalizing a standard series $M$ times, once per cube, and taking $k/M$ terms from each. We omit details in the intermediate case where the number of cubes scales at a rate slower than $k$, but we expect similar arguments to those below can be used. \\ \end{remark} First, let $\rho(x)$ denote the tensor products of a Legendre basis of order $s$, orthonormal on $[-1,1]$, i.e., tensor products of $$ \rho_j(x_\ell) = \frac{\sqrt{ j+1/2} }{2^j j!} \frac{d^j}{dx_\ell^j} (x_\ell^2-1)^j $$ for $j \in \{1,\dots,s\}$ and $\ell \in \{1,\dots,d\}$. This basis satisfies $$ \int \rho(x) \rho(x)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \ dx = I_s . $$ Now shift and rescale so that the basis is orthonormal on $M_j$ with $$ b_j(x) = 2^d \sqrt{ k} \rho\left(4k^{1/d} \left(x- \frac{1}{2} - \frac{m_j - x_0}{h} \right) \right) $$ and so satisfies \begin{align*} \int b_j(x) b_j(x)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \mathbbold{1}(x \in M_j) \ dx &=4^d k \int \rho\left(4k^{1/d} \left(x- \frac{1}{2} - \frac{m_j - x_0}{h} \right) \right) \mathbbold{1}(x \in M_j) \ dx \\ &= \int_{-1}^1 \rho(v) \rho(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \ dv = I_s \end{align*} where we used the change of variable $v = 4k^{1/d} \left(x- \frac{1}{2} - \frac{m_j - x_0}{h} \right)$ so that $dv = 4^d k \ dx$ and $x = v/4k^{1/d} + 1/2 + (m_j-x_0)/h \in M_j$ when $v \in [-1,1]^d$. Finally define the basis $$ b(v) = \{ b_1(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_1), \dots, b_k(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_k) \}^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } $$ of length $sk$. Then \begin{align*} b(v) b(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } = \begin{pmatrix} b_1(v) b_1(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_1) & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & b_2(v) b_2(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_2) & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & b_k(v) b_k(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_k) \\ \end{pmatrix} \end{align*} Therefore since $dF^*(x)$ is bounded above and below on its support, the $j$-th diagonal block of $\Omega$ is proportional to \begin{align*} \int b_j(v) b_j(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv&= I_s . \end{align*} Therefore the eigenvalues of $\Omega$ are all proportional to one and bounded as desired. Further, by the same higher-order kernel arguments for local polynomials as in Proposition \ref{prop:projbias}, the basis satisfies the \text{H\"{o}lder}{} approximation property \eqref{eq:holder}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound Q's eigenvalues by polynomial anti-concentration (Carbery-Wright) and orthonormality; build a piecewise Legendre basis on the cubes to make Omega block-diagonal. The key step is the Carbery-Wright small-ball bound for polynomials.

nodes.name: Finitely many cubes case
nodes.statement: For simplicity we only consider the case where there are exactly $k$ cubes in the local support of $F$; if there are finitely many cubes, say $M < \infty$, the arguments are more straightforward, orthonormalizing a standard series $M$ times, once per cube, and taking $k/M$ terms from each. We omit details in the intermediate case where the number of cubes scales at a rate slower than $k$, but we expect similar arguments to those below can be used. \\

nodes.name: Reduce to Gram matrix on cubes
nodes.statement: Note that since $\epsilon(1-\epsilon) \leq \pi(1-\pi) \leq 1/4$ and since $dF(x)$ is bounded above and below on its support, the eigenvalues of $Q$ will be bounded if those of the matrix $$ \sum_{j=1}^k \int \rho(v) \rho(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv $$ are, where $M_j$ indicates the $j$th disjoint cube making up the local support of $F$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the Gram matrix on the support cubes.

nodes.name: Min-max formulation
nodes.statement: By the min-max theorem, the eigenvalues are bounded by the min and max of $$ a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \int \rho(v) \rho(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \sum_j \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv \ a = \int \Big\{ a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \rho(v) \Big\}^2 \sum_j \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv $$ over all $a \in \mathbb{R}^q$ with $\| a\|=1$. First consider lower bounding the eigenvalues.
nodes.statement_short: Express eigenvalues by quadratic forms.

nodes.name: Lower eigenvalue bound
nodes.statement: Note $g(v) = a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \rho(v)$ is a polynomial of degree at most $q$. Therefore \begin{align*} \sum_j \int g(v)^2 \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv &\geq \int g(v)^2 \mathbbold{1}\{ g(v)^2 \geq \epsilon \} \sum_j \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv \\ & \geq \epsilon \int \mathbbold{1}\{ g(v)^2 \geq \epsilon \} \sum_j \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv \\ & \geq \epsilon \left\{ \sum_j \int \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv - \int \mathbbold{1}\{ g(v)^2 < \epsilon \} \ dv \right\} \\ & \geq \epsilon \left( C^* - C \epsilon^{1/2q} \right) = \left( \frac{C^*}{\sqrt{C}} \right)^{4q} > 0 \end{align*} where the last line follows since \begin{align*} \int \sum_j \mathbbold{1}( v \in M_j) \ dv & \asymp \int dF^*(v) = \int dF(x_0 + h(v-1/2)) \\ &= h^{-d} \int \mathbbold{1}\{ \|x-x_0 \| \leq h/2 \} \ dF(x) \geq C^* \end{align*} from a change of variables $x = x_0 + h(v-1/2)$, so that $v = 1/2 + (x-x_0)/h$ and $h^d \ dv = dx$, together with Assumption 1 of the lemma, and by Theorem 4 of \citet{carbery2001distributional}. The last equality follows if we choose $\epsilon =\left( C^*/2C \right)^{2q}$.
nodes.statement_short: Small-ball bound for polynomials gives a positive lower bound.

nodes.name: Upper eigenvalue bound
nodes.statement: To upper-bound the eigenvalues, note that \begin{align*} \int \Big\{ a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \rho(v) \Big\}^2 \sum_j \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv \leq \int \Big\{ a^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \rho(v) \Big\}^2 \ dv = \| a \|^2 = 1 \end{align*} since $\int \rho(v) \rho(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \ dv = I$ by the orthonormality of $\rho$.
nodes.statement_short: Orthonormality gives an upper bound of 1.

nodes.name: Plan for Omega
nodes.statement: Now consider the eigenvalues of $\Omega$. We will construct a basis of order $k$ for which eigenvalues of $\Omega$ are bounded and for which the \text{H\"{o}lder}{} approximation property \eqref{eq:holder} holds. \\ \begin{remark} For simplicity we only consider the case where there are exactly $k$ cubes in the local support of $F$; if there are finitely many cubes, say $M < \infty$, the arguments are more straightforward, orthonormalizing a standard series $M$ times, once per cube, and taking $k/M$ terms from each. We omit details in the intermediate case where the number of cubes scales at a rate slower than $k$, but we expect similar arguments to those below can be used. \\ \end{remark}
nodes.statement_short: Construct a basis for which Omega has bounded eigenvalues.

nodes.name: Legendre basis
nodes.statement: First, let $\rho(x)$ denote the tensor products of a Legendre basis of order $s$, orthonormal on $[-1,1]$, i.e., tensor products of $$ \rho_j(x_\ell) = \frac{\sqrt{ j+1/2} }{2^j j!} \frac{d^j}{dx_\ell^j} (x_\ell^2-1)^j $$ for $j \in \{1,\dots,s\}$ and $\ell \in \{1,\dots,d\}$. This basis satisfies $$ \int \rho(x) \rho(x)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \ dx = I_s . $$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce an orthonormal Legendre basis.

nodes.name: Rescaled basis per cube
nodes.statement: Now shift and rescale so that the basis is orthonormal on $M_j$ with $$ b_j(x) = 2^d \sqrt{ k} \rho\left(4k^{1/d} \left(x- \frac{1}{2} - \frac{m_j - x_0}{h} \right) \right) $$ and so satisfies \begin{align*} \int b_j(x) b_j(x)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \mathbbold{1}(x \in M_j) \ dx &=4^d k \int \rho\left(4k^{1/d} \left(x- \frac{1}{2} - \frac{m_j - x_0}{h} \right) \right) \mathbbold{1}(x \in M_j) \ dx \\ &= \int_{-1}^1 \rho(v) \rho(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \ dv = I_s \end{align*} where we used the change of variable $v = 4k^{1/d} \left(x- \frac{1}{2} - \frac{m_j - x_0}{h} \right)$ so that $dv = 4^d k \ dx$ and $x = v/4k^{1/d} + 1/2 + (m_j-x_0)/h \in M_j$ when $v \in [-1,1]^d$.
nodes.statement_short: Shift and rescale to each cube.

nodes.name: Block basis
nodes.statement: Finally define the basis $$ b(v) = \{ b_1(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_1), \dots, b_k(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_k) \}^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } $$ of length $sk$. Then \begin{align*} b(v) b(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } = \begin{pmatrix} b_1(v) b_1(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_1) & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & b_2(v) b_2(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_2) & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & b_k(v) b_k(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_k) \\ \end{pmatrix} \end{align*} Therefore since $dF^*(x)$ is bounded above and below on its support, the $j$-th diagonal block of $\Omega$ is proportional to \begin{align*} \int b_j(v) b_j(v)^{ \mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T} } \mathbbold{1}(v \in M_j) \ dv&= I_s . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Stack the cube bases; Omega is block diagonal.

nodes.name: Conclude for Omega
nodes.statement: Therefore the eigenvalues of $\Omega$ are all proportional to one and bounded as desired. Further, by the same higher-order kernel arguments for local polynomials as in Proposition \ref{prop:projbias}, the basis satisfies the \text{H\"{o}lder}{} approximation property \eqref{eq:holder}.
nodes.statement_short: Eigenvalues bounded and approximation property holds.
